findings.title: Cleanup path logs full ID batches at Error level
findings.body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags call r.log.Error on every batch (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579), including the idle batch that finds zero rows and including the full ids slice plus the SQL condition. This is leftover debug logging on a background job. At Error severity it will look like a failure in log-based alerts, and with AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize in the tens of thousands each line serializes a huge ID list, adding memory and I/O on the same path this PR is trying to keep short so MySQL locks can flush.

findings.title: All cleanup jobs now run every minute instead of every 10
findings.body: Run changes the cleanup ticker from 10 minutes to 1 minute, and this is the only change in this file. It is not mentioned in the PR and applies to every job in clean (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history), not just annotation cleanup. That multiplies database load and lock contention by about 10x, which works against the deadlock fix, and it shortens the gap relative to the 9-minute per-run timeout so a slow cleanup can overlap the next tick.

findings.title: SQLite ID list is built with quadratic string concatenation
findings.body: When the dialect is SQLite and AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is above 999, deleteByIDs inlines every selected ID with fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) inside a loop. Each step copies the entire string built so far, so a batch near the 32767 size the new test uses is O(n^2) allocations (hundreds of megabytes of copying) on the cleanup path. A strings.Builder or strings.Join would keep that fallback linear.
